Hey there! I can help you out here. I'll explain the entire process since I'm not sure how far you got. :-)

  1. In the sidebar at the bottom, under 'Administration Tools', select 'flair settings'. It should take you to a page titled "Subverse flair management interface for:".
  2. Select 'Add a new link flair'. It should redirect you to another page with a form to fill out two fields.
  3. Under 'Flair label', enter the text you want to have display in a tag that'll show up next to post titles.
  4. Under 'Flair CSS class name', enter a CSS class that'll be assigned to that specific flair. To ensure that the class name doesn't interfere with any other CSS classes WhoaVerse may have, I always prefix the class with .fl-. Example: .fl-announcement.
  5. Click the 'Add' button.
  6. Go into your subverse settings, into your custom CSS form. Start with this code:
.fl-announcement {
 display: inline-block;
}

This will activate your flair tags and it'll show up on your subverse! You can add custom styles to the flair as you wish.

Let me know if you have any questions.

I'm bipolar ... I've come a long, long way. In my late teens I would spend nights curled up in the fetal position, immobilized and crushed by the pain of emotion that swung up up up and then down down down. I came very close to suicide a couple times.

My life now is, well, fine. Calm. Level. But I still think about suicide. My relationship with it has changed. It used to be something I thought of in desperation, the only way I could think of to run away from my pain. There's no pain now. I ponder suicide rationally now. The argument typically goes, "I've done so much hard work and I still have so much farther to go. I'm tired. I can either die now or keep slogging along."

So far the costs to the people around me outweigh the potential benefit of being able to get off this ride. I feel like Atlas sometimes, carrying my own world of problems on my shoulders, unable to put them down. If it weren't for my family and my best friend, the equation would probably end up in favor of suicide. I've pretty much put away all the mythological and metaphysical concerns about suicide, like "going to hell" and all that. If I were a bad, uncaring person, I'd be so gone.

Thanks for sharing. I can relate to a lot of that. I've grown more and more tired as time passes and more of my family and friends die. I have a few really great friends left, that can understand my feelings about all of this. I know my suicide would weigh heavy on them, so I find ways to keep going, and trudging through this existence. I keep thinking one day maybe I'll have a fatal accident and it will take care of itself. Too many more years, though and I may just have to sit down with my good friends and say goodbye.

Wow, yeah. We're on the same page. I have recurring fantasies that somebody will break into my house and shoot me in the head, or I'll have an aneurism, or just ... something that takes the responsibility away from me.

It's not like I'm really depressed anymore. I'm usually in a pretty good mood, I'm not usually stressed, and by objective measure I live a decent if unproductive life, making ends meet by living with my parents because my disability payment is ridiculously insufficient. I'm a maker, and sometimes I make some pretty cool stuff.

But nevertheless, the call of the void is there. It's like being on a very, very long hike and every several miles there's a very comfy-looking sofa by the side of the trail. And I wanna sit down, but lots of people are walking with me, and they wouldn't know what to do if they went on without me. They're all so much better at walking than I am, though, and most of the people I started walking with are miles and miles ahead. The ones that are with me now have slowed down just to enjoy my company.

But I just wanna sit on that sofa, and I lost the point of all this walking years ago...

That analogy is spot on. Since my teenage years, and especially once my parents fell sick, I've felt that the walking needs justification... that for me isn't there. There's too much suffering along the path, and the path just leads to couches anyway.

Another bipolar here.

"So far the costs to the people around me outweigh the potential benefit of being able to get off this ride".

I couldn't have put it better myself. Simply put, obligations trump need to die.

I've considered a number of scenarios including making it look like an accident (I genuinely think I could get away with this), but the bottom line is that I have a duty to look after my children. Frankly, I don't know how I'm going to get through it.

I've learned a lot of tricks and tools through everything from talk therapy to mysticism to western philosophy to occultism, and it keeps me going. I've actually been thinking of writing a sort of manual, of how I do it ... I no longer have any symptoms, and that makes it a lot easier to keep going. But I'm afraid that, at the bottom of it all, there will always be that void.

I think bipolars have a different way of looking at the world, something fundamentally different. I've never met a neurotypical person who understood. Albert Camus said the only serious philosophical problem is suicide. I'm more comfortable thinking in those terms, going to those dark places, and through the lens of my mind the world tends to break down into a bunch of jagged parts that only fit together through happenstance and application of force. It's a lot harder to make peace with a world like that, you know?

But we'll do it, or else. Still, sometimes I think it's a shame that our culture has such a perverted attitude towards death and letting go. My parents give me weird looks when I tell them to stop berating my grandma for having a couple cigarettes a day, because they're terrified of the reality that she's at the end of her life. I don't think I'm callous for accepting that death is a part of life, and that shortening your life a little bit to indulge something you enjoy isn't the worst thing in the world, especially if you're aware of the consequences.

Ah well. It's late and I'm rambling. Just know that you're definitely not alone, and there are people who get it. For what it's worth.

Talk therapy, meditation, prescribed drugs, not prescribed drugs, alcohol(ism), total abstinence from all substances, yoga, running (to lose weight), lifting (to gain weight), moving job, moving country, moving continent, Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism ... I feel like I've genuinely tried to find something to suppress the desire to just stop existing.

If I'm brutally honest, parenthood was just another misguided attempt give my life some meaning. I guess it worked in a way because I'm still here and feel like I'm not going anywhere anytime soon. Although I love my children, I'm afraid I'll just get more and more cynical and resentful - and I'm already quite cynical and resentful.

The kicker is that to anyone on the outside I have a perfect life. Wife, kids (one of each flavour), house, good job, financial security. I don't necessarily think the world would be a better place without me. I don't feel ostracized or unloved. I just want out. I literally have lost the will to live and there is no real justification apart from - I don't like existing and really would rather not.

Although that was a rather self indulgent rant, it was nice to get it off my chest. I promise further contributions will be less narcissistic.

Sure. I've got some market testing and a couple weeks in Colorado between me and writing it, but since you asked you'll be one of the first to read it if/when it's done. One of the important things I've had to learn is to be comfortable with meaninglessness. Existentialism taught me how to see it and Zen and Taoism taught me how to accept it. It was one of the scariest and most perilous lessons I've learned, I think ... you may not know it, but there is a steel core within you. Survival does that to you. Bipolar gives you a front-row seat to the best and worst experiences the human condition has to offer, and there is wisdom and strength in living through both. It takes introspection to find it, but I promise you it's there.

In fact, I think that may be part of what makes us tired. For myself, I was rapid-cycling before I got myself into remission. On a bad day I would have episodes every 15 minutes - manic, depressive, and mixed. On a typical day it was every four hours. I've probably packed 40 years of life experience into the ten years since my bipolar switch got flipped. And not the good, pleasant kind of life experience people think about when they picture an old wizened man sitting in a rocker by a crackling fire. It's been balls to the wall, nonstop rollercoaster insanity. I'll bet most of us can relate to that.

I don't suppose it's any surprise to feel tired, to want out, after that. And there's no shame in it, either. Not for me nor for you. It's a hard life.

You've tried to suppress the desire to stop existing ... have you tried looking at it straight on, though? I live with mine by taking it out and polishing it up every once in a while. I treat it kind of like a sub-personality, and I argue with it periodically. I remember when it first tried arguing. It was after my life had settled down and the emotion fell away from the suicidal drive. So I took it out and examined it head-on, because I've learned that honest examination is the best (though hardest) way of dealing with the crap that comes with bipolar.

I fought it for an entire night, and it almost won. It was like the argument was a giant scale, with the pros of suicide in one basket and the cons in the other. Over the course of that night just about every con fell out of the basket, until I was down to basically two things. One, it would hurt my loved ones. Two, it's not something you can take back. In the end I couldn't will my finger to squeeze the trigger, though I did get that close.

"Facing your demons" describes my process perfectly.

But the funny thing is, after that first dangerous night, it got easier to argue the case for life. I had already "heard" all the arguments for why I should kill myself, and they get a little less compelling each time I go through them. The pro-suicide part of me likes to jump up and try to win me over every once in awhile, but I'm to the point where it takes about thirty seconds to go through the whole argument and shut him up.

have you tried looking at it straight on, though?

I have, and that's when things get hairy. I'm not sure whether you mean this metaphorically - I'll take it literally.

I like mania. When I'm manic, I'll poke the bear. I'll stand on the ledge, lean into the wind and see what happens. I'm no adrenalin junky - at least I don't think I am. I'm not doing it for the thrill - just testing the universe, if you know what I mean. A game of Russian roulette but with the odds a little more stacked against me. Two bullets in the barrel, perhaps. In the absence of god, fate (or destiny) is my higher power.

I had to stop drinking and taking drugs. They've given me, I believe, a taste of what it's like to die - and what it's like to no longer exist. The right combination and you can be lucid enough to experience that transition from alive ... to nothing ... and it feels good. They give me the cejones to go through with it. They make me forget why I'm supposed to stay alive.

Combine drugs and booze with a manic episode and eventually I'll blow my brains out (I won't really blow my brains out - that was a nod to the Russian roulette analogy - I can think of many better ways to die).

When I say to look at it straight on, I mean to do it literally but with a clear mind. It may not be something you should do until you've reached the point where your episodes are milder and you can withstand them instead of succumbing and letting them control you.

Here's what I did. For a week, I meditated before bed. My meditation consisted of asking myself over and over:

Who am I? Why am I alive? What am I living for? What's my purpose? What am I doing here?

Doing this before bed primes your subconscious to let the answers to these questions surface; normally your subconscious hides that sort of stuff to protect you.

After about a week of this, meditating at night and carefully observing my mind during the day, I broke through a wall. Suddenly it was very clear to me that my entire life was a series of opportunities turned down; that despite my illusions to the contrary, I was completely and totally mediocre and had done nothing in my entire life to be proud of.

This was news to me, and it was here that my suicidal drive spoke up. I'll personify it here, though in reality the dialogue was carried out as a train of thought:

"You've worked so hard. You've mostly stopped having episodes. You've done all this, and look at you. You're a nobody, you're small and insignificant. All your hard work has brought you to this state of mediocrity. How much harder are you going to have to work to get past your mediocrity? You thought you were halfway through the race but it turns out you only just got to the starting line. It'd be so much easier to just end it now, wouldn't it?"

And that was where the fight started. It took every last bit of strength I had to win. But I did.

I don't know if I could have survived if I had been less stable. That whole process, diving into my problems and just bearing the emotional brunt of them, seeing the reality of my situation, is kind of phase two of my recovery program. I've done it several times now, and every time I get a little stronger and make a little more progress.

Phase one was a combination of things. I had to figure out what medicines were the most effective and then find the smallest dose I could take (right now I only take 75mg of Effexor a day and some klonopin as needed). I spent six months with a therapist learning the process of rational emotive behavior therapy. I learned about chaos magick's tenet of belief shifting, and I put that together with the REBT to develop a method to literally tinker with and change my personality and beliefs. I used that belief shifting to instill concepts from eastern philosophy into my personality, and I'm still tinkering with myself to this day. It was the belief shifting that got me to a point where I was stable and strong enough to really examine my core self in phase two and break it down so I could rebuild it.

That probably sounds a little fantastical, but it works...

But did you win? Or did you just convinced yourself not to die. Maybe that was victory for you ... I'm certainly not trying to instigate some sort of pissing contest over who wants to die the most. I guess maybe I don't want to convince myself not to die. Ugh, double negative.

My shrink is trying to get me on lithium. He tells me it's very effective at taking away suicidal thoughts. I've resisted so far because perversely I'm not convinced I want these thoughts to go away. Much of the time I barely have the mental capacity for rational thought. And I'm worried that lithium will snuff out the microscopic ember of clear thinking I still have.

I'm actually fascinated with lithium. You know, locations where the groundwater has a relatively higher than normal concentration of lithium (we're still talking about trace dosages though) generally have happier people, lower crime, and better health. If I ever judge that my Effexor isn't having the effect I want, I'll be trying out lithium. A low dosage, though. Medicine's something you want to keep to a minimum if possible. I've found that, while it'll round out episodes, too much medicine will also halt my emotional growth by taking me out of touch with my emotional state altogether. You want just enough to take the edge off the episodes, to make it easier to deal with them as you work through the faulty programming in your mind that's causing your emotions to swing wildly.

I'm alive, so I consider it a win. I don't consider it a failing that I still live with suicidal thoughts. It's a part of my existence right now, and to lament it would only make it harder to deal with.

I find it completely plausible that you wouldn't want to let go of your suicidal drive. If you examine it closely, you'll probably find that there is a measure of comfort in the familiarity of the feelings. And getting rid of them, or at least making them a smaller part of your life, may feel like a sacrifice. That's a normal part of changing your beliefs and emotions. What you have now always feels safer and easier than any changes you would make, even when it's the changes that would make your life safer and easier. It takes a high level of pragmatism to give up the parts of you that cause your symptoms: it's learning to reject beliefs that make your life worse and adopt ones that make your life better. The medicine, taken in moderation, is a helpful (and often necessary) part of a larger recovery program, but bipolar symptoms start and end in the mind.

yes and yes. And not for the reasons you might think. I honestly believe that in a world where they didn't exist I would be any less suicidal. It's easy, even logical, to assume that they contribute to me feeling like I do. But the truth is, they are the only reason I'm alive. I felt this way long before I got married and had children.

I really do love them, you know. But I was selfish to have them ... I thought things might change, but they haven't. My children are my reason to live, or maybe they're my excuse not to die. I may never find out because despite how I feel - for the moment anyway - I don't think I could abandon them.

I will never have a wife or children myself. I've already gotten myself a vasectomy to make sure of it.

However I made a promise to my mom that I will not kill myself as long as she is still living. After that it's completely fair game. Other than that I am not obligated to any other shit. I live only for myself and nobody else.

I'm also an organ donor. I'll make sure to call 911 and let them know I'm checking out.

Honestly I don't see any other way that I'm leaving this world. Either I die from a motorcycle accident, or by my own hands.

Committed child-free here, too. Obviously, I don't feel that the overall experience itself outweighs the suffering you're exposed to through conscious existence.

After my parents died and then some close friends, I really thought that was the end for me. I still feel that way a lot. My last remaining close friends keep me around, but I walk the line pretty hard with that. I also deal with the cowardice of actually performing the act. My inner drive for survival seems to keep me from the final act. It's a bunch of horseshit, that I'm trying to overcome in my mind.
Too bad the handful of childfree people can't stop the world population from growing to 7+ billion.

Too bad, indeed. I lived my life in a bubble of pre-confirmed social norms, until I met my first sociology professor. I had heard about over population, but he introduced me to exponential population growth, and I just sunk.

When I went home and asked my parents about their motives for having children, they told me they wanted someone to help take care of them in their old age. That worked out for them, as I got to watch them degrade and die at their bedsides.

We've made too many mouths, that continue to recite the social norms and there's no saving it now.
Something of a cliche, but do you resent your parents - as in, would you rather have never been born? Can you recall a point in your life when being alive hasn't felt like such a chore?

In a way. I wish they would have thought harder about what life means, and not just acted out the common routine. I do wish I had never been born. Parts of my childhood were lighter and more carefree, but even then I remember lying in bed many nights and worrying about my family, because we were poor and it caused my parents to struggle and suffer much more than they should have. Then as I got a little older and starting realizing (and being shown) the true implications of life... how entropy dominates and everything degrades, it's only become heavier.

For what it's worth, I really wish I'd thought harder about what life means - maybe your parents did too.

Ironically, up until my 30s, I was vehemently against the idea of having children. It was as though a switch was flicked in my brain and procreating suddenly became desirable. More than that actually. Essential.

I wonder whether my kids will be resentful towards me as they get older. I hope not. I hope they can be happy. I hope they're not wired like me.

Well, if it's any consolation, even with my critical perspective on what decisions my parents made, I do love them more than all of that. They were good to me and they did their best to make life good for us. They were victims of this existence just as much as I am, I just wish the buck would have stopped at them, instead of me. Hell, I wish the buck would have stopped long ago, so that they wouldn't have had to suffer either.

Do you think your parents ever felt like you though? You mention their struggle but I guess for many, that's part of the life experience. Can't appreciate the highs if you don't have the lows ... and all that jazz.

My dad's dad died when he was young, like me, and there were many times he would be depressed and talk a little bit about it. My mom had a horrible childhood, where her mom killed herself, but she clung to religion and our family to keep her spirits up. I think they both thought that they could find happiness in family, and they did to a certain extent, but inevitably just perpetuated the cycle. My dad had a moment, when he was sick, that he apologized to me and said that he remembered being young and thinking he'd never get old and sick. I think that mentality drives a lot of people, and then time catches up to all of us while we're trying to distract ourselves and play our roles.
